GLOSSARY
attention restoration — the finding, published by Rachel and

Stephen Kaplan in 1989, that the effortful kind of attention is a finite supply which runs down with use, and that what refills it is not rest but the other kind — the kind a thing takes from you without your having to force it.

compassion fatigue — the particular way people in caring work come apart: not from the hours, or the paperwork, or the employer, but from the caring itself. Taken up by Charles Figley in 1995, after Carla Joinson had put the phrase into print three years earlier, in a nursing magazine, writing about emergency wards.
continuity appointment — a real scheduling category, for a patient who should go on seeing the same clinician. It is not a category for a conversation nobody needs.

directed attention — the Kaplans’ name for the kind of attention you have to force, which William James had called voluntary, as against the kind a thing takes from you by itself — James’s involuntary attention, which the Kaplans renamed fascination.
The first runs out. The second costs nothing.

dissociation [dih-soh-see-AY-shun] — the clinical term for the sense of being slightly apart from yourself, watching yourself act. It is a symptom in some conditions and a drug effect in others. In the case of ketamine it is not a side effect; it is the mechanism.
exception queue — in a system that handles most cases itself, the cases it declines to handle, set aside for a person. A real term, and not coined to be cruel.

ketamine [KET-uh-meen] — an anaesthetic, in hospitals and ambulances since the 1960s. At doses far below the surgical one it has become a standard treatment for depression that has not answered to anything else, and it works, and nobody is entirely sure why.

MDMA — the compound sold recreationally as ecstasy. Not a hallucinogen. What it does is shorten the ordinary distance between a person and whoever is in front of them, which is why it has been trialled for post-traumatic stress and why its effects do not survive repetition.
nodule [NOD-yool] — a small rounded lump in tissue. Most are nothing. The work of reading a scan is in large part the work of deciding which.
preliminary read — a first pass over a scan, flagging what a second reader should look at. It is not a diagnosis and it is not signed.

psilocybin [sil-oh-SY-bin] — the active compound in certain mushrooms. Trialled at Johns Hopkins and New York University in people facing death from cancer, where a single supervised dose was found to reduce the fear of dying for months afterwards.

Simone Weil [see-MOHN VAY] — French philosopher, 1909–1943, who held that attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity, and that the whole of loving your neighbour consists in being able to ask them what they are going through and to wait for the answer.
SPIKES — a six-step protocol for delivering bad news, published in 2000 by Walter Baile, Robert Buckman and colleagues, and taught in medical schools since. Setting, Perception, Invitation,
Knowledge, Emotions, Strategy. It is good, and it is honest about what it does not cover.
the eighteen seconds — the finding, by Howard Beckman and

Richard Frankel in 1984, that where a doctor interrupts a patient’s opening account, the average time to the interruption is eighteen seconds. When the work was done again in 2018 the figure was eleven.
THE OBSERVATION
The second year

Attention is not something a person has. It is something a person spends, and what it is made of is time out of a life that is not getting it back. Nobody ever invoiced for it, so nobody ever counted it, so for as long as there have been people it has looked free.

Then it was counted. Not the spending, which cannot be seen from outside, but the shape of it, which can — a pause of the right length, a silence nobody steps into, a voice with no hurry in it. That shape turns out to be cheap. It can be made perfectly, and made again, and made at four in the morning on the nine hundredth occasion, by something that is not spending anything at all.

I lost to it and the score was fair, and that is the part I keep going back over. Nothing was taken from me. I gave it away an hour at a time, to people who needed it and who will not remember my name, and I would do it again tomorrow — and at no point did anyone, myself included, think to write down what it came to.
I do not know how much of what makes us human is of the second kind. I have started to think it is most of it.
